newsitem.title: UK: Tactical voters plan their attack in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Tactical voters plan their attack in UK election.

text.p: Britain's election on Thursday could be determined by people who choose to vote for a party they do no not actually support.

Political analysts say tactical voting, where people vote for whichever party has the best chance of unseating the ruling Conservatives, could have a significant effect in closely-fought "marginal" seats where the election result will be decided.
"It could have a pretty dramatic impact in marginal seats," said Neil Carter, lecturer in politics at York University. "I think there's going to be a lot of it."
Tactical voting has resulted from the "first-past-the-post" electoral system in Britain and an overriding aim among some voters to ensure the Conservatives are ousted after 18 years.
Only the winning candidate in each of its 659 geographical constituencies gets a seat in parliament. Votes cast for the losing candidates are ignored. Labour needs a uniform 4.3 percent swing to win.

Supporters of tactical voting say that, rather than "wasting" votes on candidates with little hope of success, anti-Conservative voters should rally round the party with the best chance of defeating the Conservatives in each area.

A campaign has been set up to coordinate anti-Conservative tactical voting, urging voters to choose the party that came second to the Conservatives in each constituency in the 1992 election, whether it is the main opposition Labour Party, the Liberal Democrats or the Scottish and Welsh nationalists.
Get Rid of Them (GROT) says it has only one aim: "To get as many Conservatives as possible out of parliament by means of intelligent tactical voting at the next general election."
Britain's Observer and Guardian newspapers have also thrown its weight behind an anti-Conservative voting strategy.
The Observer has published a guide to the party most likely to defeat the Conservatives in each seat and urged readers to vote accordingly.
Political analysts say tactical voting may play a larger part in this election than any other British poll in history.

"The electorate has become more educated and informed about the possibilities of tactical voting," Carter at York University said. "And because Labour and the Liberal Democrats have moved closer in terms of policies, voters will be less reluctant to switch from one to the other."

Neither Labour nor the Liberal Democrats are prepared to publicly endorse tactical voting, although Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown has tacitly agreed it could help his party add to its 26 seats in parliament.
But in many constituencies, candidates try to win votes by claiming to have the best chance of beating the Conservatives.
This has led to friction in regions where the Liberal Democrats came second in 1992 but where the Labour Party says it has now gained ground to become the main challenger.

"It is not always obvious that the candidate who came second last time is the one to vote for, and that might muddy the waters," Carter said. "But in many seats its will be obvious who to vote for, and it could be very significant."
